g8-2023-015.activity: Exponent Rules With Bases Other than 10
g8-2023-015.quote: practice using exponent rules to analyze expressions and identify equivalent expressions
g8-2023-015.why: The item asks which of four (2^a)^b expressions equals 1/16, so it needs the power-of-a-power and negative-exponent rules applied to base 2 and then read as a fraction. This activity has students work down four lists of expressions with bases 5, 3, x and 8, including negative exponents, deciding which are equivalent to the original -- the same equivalence-hunting the item asks for, and this lesson is the one that establishes that the rules hold for bases other than 10 (its Activity 1 builds the base-2 table and asks for 1/32 as a power of 2). The losing reading's Negative Exponent Table is the right rule but only ever in base 10, which is exactly the generalisation the item turns on.

g8-2023-022.quote: Draw as many different triangles as you can with each of these sets of measurements
g8-2023-022.why: The item gives one angle of 34 degrees and asks which pair of angles could be the other two -- i.e. which set of three angle measures can actually be a triangle. This is the only activity in the grade 7 unit built on three given ANGLES: one set (50, 60, 70) yields many triangles and the other (50, 60, 100) yields none, which is precisely the possible/impossible judgement the item wants. The losing reading's 2 Angles and 1 Side asks how many different triangles share three measures, a uniqueness question rather than a feasibility-of-three-angles question.

g8-2023-038.activity: Reflecting Points on the Coordinate Plane
g8-2023-038.quote: generalize to describe where a reflection over the y-axis takes any point
g8-2023-038.why: The item reflects C(-4, 3) over the y-axis and asks for the coordinates of C'. This activity has students reflect a list of labelled points over an axis, label each image with its coordinates, and then generalise the rule for reflecting any point over the y-axis -- the item's question with the item's line of reflection. The losing reading's Dilations and Slope Triangles is about dilating a triangle from a centre to build a line, and never touches reflection.

g8-2023-043.why: The item is a bare 'what value of x makes the equation true', tagged NY-8.EE.7b. This is the lesson the guides tag NY-8.EE.7.b, and its second activity is the plainest instance of the item's task: three equations with rational coefficients, distribution and variables on both sides, to be solved for x (the reading named this lesson but quoted its narrative about comparing solution paths; the task statement is the better warrant). Trading Moves in the next lesson asks for essentially the same solving, but framed as a partner routine of describing each move, so it is a near-miss rather than a wrong answer.

g8-2023-045.quote: What is the value of the rate of change for each situation
g8-2023-045.why: The item shows one function as a table and one as a graph and asks which has the greater rate of change, with both rates stated. This activity pairs relationships given in different representations (equation vs. description, description vs. table) and asks, twice, who earns more and 'what is the value of the rate of change for each situation' -- the item's exact two-part demand, in required work. The losing reading's An Illuminated Moon is a single-context modelling task whose point is that a linear model fails, and it compares nothing; the only closer rival, Unit 5 Lesson 8's 'Which Is Growing Faster?', is an optional activity.

g8-2024-010.quote: Cone with a height of 8 centimeters and a radius of 3 centimeters
g8-2024-010.why: The item asks for an expression for the difference between the volume of a sphere of radius 4 and a cone of radius 3 and height 8 -- two formulas applied to figures whose dimensions are unrelated. Lesson 21 is the only required place where cone, cylinder and sphere formulas are used side by side, and this activity literally sets a cone of height 8 and radius 3 against a sphere and asks which holds the given volume; its weakness is that it is an optional activity, and the lesson's required Information Gap links a cone and a sphere only through matched dimensions. The losing reading's Spheres in Cylinders derives 4/3 pi r^3 for a sphere inscribed in a cylinder, which supplies one formula but never asks the item's compare-and-subtract question.

g8-2024-045.quote: Find the slope of the line that passes through each pair of points
g8-2024-045.why: The item gives two ordered pairs of a linear function and asks for the rate of change, nothing else. This Cool-down is that question verbatim, three times over, including a pair with 0 as an x-coordinate and pairs with negatives, and it is where the lesson tests the general slope procedure it has just built. The losing reading's An Illuminated Moon does use two data points, but inside a modelling task whose purpose is to discover that the linear model breaks down.

g8-2025-035.activity: Similar Triangles on the Same Line
g8-2025-035.quote: The grid shows three right triangles, each with its longest side on the same line
g8-2025-035.why: The item shows two students drawing different slope triangles on the same line, getting 2/3 and 4/6, and asks whether both are right. This activity puts three right triangles with their longest sides on one line, has students show the triangles are similar, fill in a table of (vertical) / (horizontal) for each, and say why the column is constant -- the exact reason both students are correct. The losing reading's Toward a More General Slope Formula derives slope from coordinates, which computes a slope but does not address why different triangles on one line agree.

g8-2025-037.quote: rational approximations of irrational numbers to place both rational and irrational numbers
g8-2025-037.why: The item asks where sqrt(4) + sqrt(10) sits on a number line, which needs sqrt(10) approximated between 3 and 4 and the sum located. This activity has students plot the solutions of x^2 = 3, y^2 = 16 and z^2 = 30 on a number line -- a perfect square alongside two irrational roots -- and the lesson's preceding activity pins each root between consecutive whole numbers, which is the estimation the item rewards. The losing reading's Square Root of 3 also approximates a root, but by drawing a square on a grid rather than by placing values on a number line.

g8-2025-039.quote: Find the slope of the line that passes through each pair of points
g8-2025-039.why: The item gives a table of values for a linear function and asks for the rate of change, which is done by taking any two rows as a pair of points. This Cool-down asks for exactly that computation on three pairs of points, and it is where the lesson tests the general slope procedure. The losing reading's An Illuminated Moon is a modelling task built to show a linear model failing, not a rate-of-change computation.

g8-2025-046.activity: Reflecting Points on the Coordinate Plane
g8-2025-046.quote: when reflecting over the vertical or horizontal axis, one coordinate value must stay the same
g8-2025-046.why: The item reflects triangle ABC over the y-axis and asks for the coordinates of A'. This activity has students plot points, reflect them over an axis, label each image with its coordinates, and generalise the sign change for reflection over the y-axis -- the item's question. The losing reading's Dilations and Slope Triangles concerns dilating a triangle to generate points on a line and never reflects anything.

g8-2026-001.quote: Select all of the translations that take Triangle T to Triangle U
g8-2026-001.why: The item translates A(-2, 3) four left and two up and asks for the coordinates of A'. Lesson 5 is the coordinate-transformation lesson (NY-8.G.3), and this Warm-up is its only translation task, matching translations to the coordinate pairs that describe them; the rest of the lesson supplies the same coordinate bookkeeping for reflections and rotations. The losing reading's Dilations and Slope Triangles is a dilation activity in the slope unit and has nothing to do with translating a figure.

g8-2026-005.quote: how they might figure out a value for π using measurements of circles
g8-2026-005.why: The item asks which of 0, pi, sqrt(9) and 1/3 is irrational, so it turns on pi being irrational while a whole-number-valued square root is not. This is the only activity in the curriculum that treats pi as an irrational number, contrasting it with numbers that have a fractional representation; its neighbour, Rational Numbers as Fractions, deliberately includes a rational square root to kill the sqrt(9) distractor. The losing reading's Looking for a Solution is where 'irrational' is coined, but only via the hunt for a fraction whose square is 2 -- it never mentions pi, so it defines the word without asking the item's question.

g8-2026-011.lessonTitle: Tables, Equations, and Graphs of Functions
g8-2026-011.quote: a graph in which each input does not give exactly one output
g8-2026-011.why: The item shows four graphs and asks which relation is not a function -- a graphical, vertical-line-test judgement. This activity puts a runner's graph that is a function beside one where a runner returns to the start, producing a graph in which each input does not give exactly one output, and the lesson's goal is stated as deciding whether a GRAPH represents a function. The losing reading's You Know This, Do You Know That? is where the one-output-per-input idea is defined, but entirely from verbal situations, with no graphs in sight.

g8-2026-012.quote: determine whether it has no solutions, exactly one solution, or is true for all
g8-2026-012.why: The item gives four equations, three of which have exactly one solution and one of which is an identity after distributing, and asks which has infinitely many solutions. This activity gives fifteen equations -- several needing distribution, such as 1/4(12 - 4x) = 3 - x -- and asks for each whether it has no solution, one solution, or infinitely many: the item's three-way sort. The losing reading's Thinking About Solutions sorts into only two bins, always-true and never-true, so it cannot produce the item's one-solution distractors.

g8-2026-020.quote: Using what you know about similar triangles, find an equation for the line
g8-2026-020.why: The item asks for the equation of the line through (0, 9) and (3, 0), which means getting the slope from two points and recognising the y-intercept. This activity is the curriculum's one 'write an equation for a line from two labelled points' task, and it goes on to test candidate points against that equation, which is the same reasoning the distractors probe. The losing reading's All the Same is about the equations of horizontal and vertical lines (y = -4, x = 3), a lesson whose whole subject is the one kind of line the item is not about.

g8-2026-025.quote: Find two pairs of angles in the diagram that have the same measure
g8-2026-025.why: The item rotates triangle ABC to XYZ and asks which angle congruence statement is correct, so it needs the correspondence of vertices under the rotation plus the fact that angles are preserved. This activity asks which points in the image correspond to A, B and C under each rigid transformation and then to find pairs of angles with the same measure and justify them -- the narrative calls recognising corresponding angles of equal measure the point of the task. The losing reading's Rotating a Segment is about what a 180-degree rotation does to a segment and never pairs up corresponding angles.

g8-2026-026.quote: Determine the vertical intercept and explain what it represents in this situation
g8-2026-026.why: The item shows a graphed linear function and asks for its rate of change and its y-intercept, with distractors that swap the two and flip the sign. This Cool-down asks for exactly both readings off a graph, and the lesson's main activity is built on a student who swaps the initial value and the rate -- the item's distractor structure. The losing reading's Recycling asks students to sketch a linear model over data and judge where it predicts well, which is modelling rather than reading slope and intercept off a line.
